# Advertiser conversions

Advertisers report business events (purchases, sign-ups, anything else) to
`POST /api-conversion/v1/events` as `{ "data": [ ...events ] }`, check a checkout code with
`POST /api-conversion/v1/referral-codes/verify` and send visitors through
`GET /cta/{link_token}`. The wire names follow the Meta and TikTok event APIs (`event_name`,
`event_time` in Unix seconds, `event_id`, `event_source_url`, `client_user_agent`,
`client_ip_address`, and Meta's own `fbp`/`fbc`). Money, the conversion-page URL, the converting
browser and the prehashed customer details are top-level fields here; provider-specific nested
payloads are not accepted. `ev_click_id` and `referral_code` are ours. An event may carry any
combination of a click id, a referral code, both or neither — with only browser data — and every
one is stored and, when eligible, forwarded. The code is the contract: `src/partnerApi/createConversionHttpRouter.ts` (routes,
status codes, error reasons, rate limits), `input/validateConversionEventInput.ts` (the event
schema), `attribution/evaluateConversionAttribution.ts` (rule `click-v1`),
`referral/selectUsableConversionReferralCodes.ts` (which codes an integration may use, the rule
ingestion credits by and verification answers by),
`referral/verifyConversionReferralCodes.ts` (what a partner learns about a code) and
`meta/evaluateMetaConversionDelivery.ts` (what may leave for Meta). This domain is independent
of `marketing_event`, application sessions and the product analytics catalog, which are
Evangelist's own.

Keep the Notion Conversion API draft and PR description derived from these implementations,
and update them when behavior changes. Describe implemented behavior and its current limits;
label unimplemented proposals separately. The original design plan does not override the code.

## Ad platform providers

Everything specific to one paid platform sits behind `conversionProvider.ts`: one
`ConversionProvider` per `apps.ad_platform` value, registered in `conversionProviders.ts`
(`CONVERSION_PROVIDERS`). A provider owns three run-time capabilities, plus a report dispatch, and
nothing outside its adapter directory reaches into them. The kernel's own event facts — browser
context and customer hashes — are provider-neutral, so a later destination (another ad platform,
an analytics or CRM tool) reads the same facts through its own adapter:

- **click** — the query parameter the platform appends to an ad's destination (`fbclid` for Meta),
  how a value is validated, and how the observed value is stored beside the click
  (`apps.meta_conversion_click`) and read back for delivery. `links/buildConversionRedirect` strips
  every provider's parameter from the tracking URL, forwards the valid ones to the destination and
  hands them to `links/recordConversionClick`, which records each through its provider. The
  provider also names `networks`, the CIDR ranges its own systems fetch from, which
  `links/classifyConversionClick` records as ignored (`ad_platform_network`).
- **event** — the identifiers the platform's own browser tag sets, which an advertiser reports with
  an event (`fbp` and `fbc` for Meta): their top-level field names and syntax checks, and how an
  accepted event's values are stored beside it (`apps.meta_conversion_event`).
  `input/validateConversionEventInput` takes those fields out of the item before the kernel's strict
  schema (so an unknown field is still rejected), the fingerprint includes them as
  `providerIdentifiers`, and ingestion hands them to the platform inside the event's transaction,
  only for the insert that won. The platform's `prepare` reads them back; nothing else does. A
  platform field name must never collide with a kernel field or another platform's.
- **delivery** — `findDestination` takes a `ConversionDeliveryRoute` (`{ campaignId?, brandId }`)
  and names where those events go (a ready, unpaused `apps.meta_integration` — see
  `services/metaIntegration/AGENTS.md`): the campaign's own integration for an event credited to a
  campaign, and the advertiser's default (`apps.brand.unattributed_meta_integration_id`) for an event
  credited to none. **Campaign routing never falls back**: a credited event whose campaign selects
  no usable integration is delivered nowhere, rather than into its advertiser's default, because
  the default exists for events no campaign earned. `delivery/enqueueConversionDeliveries` queues
  one `apps.conversion_delivery` row per provider inside the ingestion transaction; `prepare`
  decides at send time whether a claimed row is sent, skipped or failed and builds the send. It decides
  from the kernel's facts — `delivery/loadConversionDeliveryFacts` reads the event and the click
  it named, with the observed browser context, once per attempt under the outbox row's lock — plus
  the rows only the platform keeps (its destination, its click identifier); an adapter never reads
  `conversion_event` or `conversion_click` itself, and the kernel has already skipped an ignored
  event (`event_ignored`) before asking. `configurationErrorCodes` names the stored failure codes
  whose pending retries need an operator's configuration repair; the alert reader matches both
  provider and code. The outbox, claim lease, sweep and completion in `delivery/` are
  provider-neutral, keyed by `(conversion_event_id, provider)`.
- **reporting** — not part of the run-time contract. The campaign's aggregate delivery stages and
  per-ad breakdown, in the platform's own vocabulary (`meta/getMetaCampaignConversionDelivery`,
  `meta/getMetaCampaignConversionAdBreakdown`), are registered per platform in
  `reporting/conversionPaidReportingProviders` — a dispatch point whose shapes are Meta-shaped by
  decision, not a proven abstraction. `reporting/getCampaignPaidDeliveryReport` dispatches on the
  campaign paid boost's `ad_platform_id` and reports no stages and no ads for a campaign without a boost.

The Meta adapter lives in `meta/`. Another runtime platform needs an adapter directory, a registry
entry, its `apps.ad_platform` enum value and any click- or event-identifier side table keyed by the
row it extends. Generic ingestion, redirect and delivery compose that interface. Reporting vocabulary and additional
tracking methods need separate design; the runtime interface does not make those provider-neutral.

## Tables

Credentials carry a required advertiser foreign key (`brand_id`); links retain a nullable one.
The migration assigns existing credentials to the static `evangelist` advertiser and makes the
column NOT NULL. Evangelist follows the same ownership checks as every other advertiser.
New admin credentials require an explicit active advertiser; rotations inherit it. The credential
insert trigger supports old versions that omit the field: roots receive `evangelist`, and successors
inherit the namespace root's advertiser under the same lock used by rotation. There is no column
default or management API to change credential ownership. Existing attribution and fingerprints
remain immutable.
Generated links snapshot their post's campaign advertiser (a live Meta ad's composite post FK also
pins its campaign). Migration backfill and a binding-insert trigger share an ownership resolver:
manual links use the current post, Meta links use the matching live ad or verified original
creation provenance after ad deletion. Unknown generated owners and unbound manual links remain
null. The trigger covers old API writers during rolling deployment. Assigned
link ownership is immutable, so moving a post cannot transfer existing visitor context. Campaign
reports include only links whose advertiser matches the current campaign's advertiser; unresolved
owners remain excluded until verified operator repair establishes ownership. Events must also have
an accepting credential with that advertiser before contributing revenue, dimensions, landing
confirmation or customer identities. Historical foreign-credential attribution remains stored for
provenance, but contributes none of those report facts; its owned-link redirect still counts.
Delivery applies the same advertiser boundary to the current campaign before naming a route or
forwarding post labels. A post moved to another advertiser leaves its original click and receipt
attribution intact, but cannot route that advertiser's event to the new campaign. The remaining
owned referral campaign, or the accepting advertiser's default when no owned campaign remains,
supplies the existing fallback. Ingestion, send-time facts, SQL recovery routing and destination
lookups all enforce this; an old delivery pinned elsewhere still must pass the destination check.
Deploy schema, verify each integration's credential/link owners, then finish updating every API/worker
before using the new frontend management surfaces. The shared deployment workflow runs application
jobs in parallel; wait for successful API validation and frontend deployment before onboarding integrations.
Existing credentials belong to Evangelist; other advertisers need newly issued credentials. The
triggers preserve snapshots across versions; old application versions still lack the advertiser
checks, so they cannot provide isolation during the overlap.
`apps.campaign_conversion_link` binds tracking links to an existing `(channel_platform_id, post_id)`
pair through a composite `apps.post` foreign key. Both fields are required; there is no campaign ID
column. All campaign scopes join both fields to the current post. A link generated for an ad also
records the ad platform and local ad it was made for (`ad_platform_id` and `ad_id`, both set or both
null), which is what makes it a paid source. Manual links have no campaign scope until bound
to a post by an operator, independently of their advertiser snapshot; there is no campaign-link management UI. Config (operator-managed): `global.api_credential` (one HMAC
credential and its event namespace), `apps.conversion_link` (a
public tracking link), `apps.meta_integration` (an agency's Meta dataset, selected per campaign
through `apps.campaign.meta_integration_id` — the one place a campaign's conversions are delivered
to, owned by `services/metaIntegration/`) and
`apps.conversion_referral_code` (the registry of codes an audience types at checkout). The
redirect also reads the query parameters a campaign's Conversion goal chose, which the paid-boost
domain keeps with the goal's destination in `apps.campaign_paid_boost_conversion`
(`../paidBoost/AGENTS.md`; the vocabulary is `links/conversionRedirectParams.ts`).
Data (written by traffic and the sweep): `apps.conversion_click`
(one visit, id is the public `ev_click_id`, the one home of its observed IP and User-Agent),
`apps.meta_conversion_click` (only the `fbclid` seen on that visit), `apps.conversion_event` (the event as accepted, with `attributed_click_id` and `attributed_referral_code_id`),
`apps.meta_conversion_event` (only the `fbp`/`fbc` an advertiser reported with that event) and
`apps.conversion_delivery` (the delivery outbox: one row per event and ad platform, pinned to the
provider destination it was queued for). Meta specifics only ever live in `meta_*` tables keyed by
the row they extend.

A referral code is config, like a link: one row is one spelling, owned by one campaign and
optionally labelled with the creator channel that hands it out (`channel_platform_id` plus
`channel_platform_unique_account_handle`, both or neither — deliberately **no** channel foreign
key, because an external campaign hands out codes for channels this system has never verified).
A **personal** code also carries `user_id`, the creator it was generated for; a partial unique
index on `(campaign_id, user_id)` allows one per creator and campaign, and codes without an owner
are unaffected by it. A code without either label already attributes conversions, and a label
filled in later applies to the history the row already credited without changing any event or
attribution ID. Whether a campaign uses codes at all is `apps.campaign.enable_referral_codes`, set
in the create wizard, cloned with the campaign and switchable on the admin campaign detail while
the campaign is scheduled or live (`campaign/updateCampaignSettings`): it gates who is issued one,
which codes ingestion credits and verification answers (one statement,
`referral/selectUsableConversionReferralCodes`), what the report counts (below) and whether the
submission worker accepts it as a bio proof. `code` is
unique across the whole table and
`collate "C"`, so the unique index and every equality are byte-exact whatever the database
collation is. Case-insensitivity comes from the application, which lowercases the submitted
spelling before its lookup — never `lower()` in the query, which would give up the index — so a
code resolves only when it is **stored lowercase**, and the database does not check that.
`disabled_at` stops a code attributing without touching what it already credited. `metadata` is
the code's optional **advertiser-facing payload**: attribution and reporting do not read it, and
the verify endpoint and the events receipt return it verbatim to the code's advertiser, so it must
never hold internal-only data (that belongs in `origin`, which never leaves the system).
`conversion_event.attributed_referral_code_id` is a real
foreign key to that row, so a rename moves nothing and a registry row cannot be deleted out from
under an event; a check constraint keeps it null unless the receipt also kept the submitted
`referral_code`.

Credentials, links, clicks, events, deliveries, `meta_conversion_click` rows and referral codes have
nullable `origin jsonb` for internal provenance (as does `apps.meta_integration`;
`meta_conversion_event`, `campaign_conversion_link` and `campaign_conversion_funnel` have none). Creation of E2E
credentials and links sets `{ "is_test_data": true }`; normal creation defaults to null.
Click `origin.request` records bounded, allowlisted tracking query parameters, a referrer
origin/path without its query or fragment, and `headers`: the allowlisted request headers that tell
a person's navigation from a fetcher's (`CLICK_HEADER_NAMES` in `links/captureConversionClickContext`
— language, client hints, fetch metadata, prefetch/preview markers, `x-requested-with`, the
`x-forwarded-for` chain and Front Door's `x-azure-*` peer headers), each at most 512 characters.
Never cookies, authorization or any other header. They are diagnostics only: nothing classifies,
attributes or delivers by them.
Both `conversion_click` and `conversion_event` carry `ignore boolean not null default false`: rows
kept for provenance that are not advertiser traffic. A click is ignored when
`links/classifyConversionClick` names it — the `fbclid=test` of a Test CTA (`test_click`), a
link-preview / ad-review User-Agent (`crawler`), or an address inside an ad platform's own networks
(`ad_platform_network`: the provider's `click.networks`, for Meta the AS32934 snapshot in
`meta/metaNetworks`, because Meta's ad review fetches the link with ordinary browser User-Agents and
fresh `fbclid`s) — with the reason in `origin.ignore_reason`. The platforms' own ranges are the only
addresses that classify, an owner decision of 24 Sep 2026 that replaced "never the source address";
other clouds a review may use still count. An event is ignored when its batch envelope carried `"test": true` (inside
the signed body, so nothing in transit can flip it) or a click it is allowed to use is ignored,
attributed or not. Foreign clicks and unassigned links cannot supply this flag to a
credential. Ingestion queues no delivery row for an ignored event, and the delivery kernel terminally
skips (`event_ignored`) any row a backfill flags after queuing, before any provider is asked. The flag is decided once, at
record time, and is not part of event identity. Every count, funnel and ROAS figure must filter `ignore = false`; the read
models expose it.
Three things are called "test" here, and they are independent. **Test data** is
`origin.is_test_data` on E2E fixture credentials and links: fixture ownership, selected only by
`whereConversionTestData`; the live sweep skips it and fixture readback keeps it. The campaign
Conversion preview excludes these fixtures except its own explicitly marked simulated data
(`origin.source = 'testing_campaign_conversions'`). **Test traffic** is
`ignore = true` on a click or event: never delivered, left out of every count. A **test click** is
an operator's Test CTA visit, the one kind of test traffic the product creates itself. The
harness's own clicks and events stay `ignore = false` on purpose, so the recording delivery can
assert the Meta request.
A generated link's `origin` snapshots the original ad, ad set, campaign and post IDs; its binding's
`ad_id` is plain text that survives ad-only deletion, preserving attribution while the post exists.
Hard post deletion removes the link and its conversion data, except events a referral code credits,

content.content:
which keep their row with `attributed_click_id` cleared. Origin is never
accepted as a blob from partner requests or included in partner responses or
Meta payloads. Credential origin controls delivery isolation; link origin controls fixture
ownership. These are exact JSON boolean checks. The generic predicate is
`services/db/whereTestDataOrigin.ts` (`whereTestDataOrigin`, `isTestDataOrigin`), because
`origin.is_test_data` is the shared provenance convention of every table that has an `origin`
column rather than a conversion fact — `apiCredential/rotateApiCredential` asks it without
importing this domain. `conversionTestData.ts` is this domain's vocabulary over it:
`whereConversionTestData` (the sweep's and the harness's filter), `isConversionTestData` (the
same check read as a column) and `whereConversionReportable` (what campaign reporting counts: live
rows plus the campaign generator's own `CONVERSION_SIMULATION_SOURCE` fixtures). Null, a missing
key, false, or the string `"true"` do not mark a row as test data; no query spells the check out
inline. Editing a link preserves its creation origin.

## Identity

- `(client_event_namespace, client_event_id)` is the deduplication key. A credential issued from
  scratch is its own namespace (`client_event_namespace` is its id); `rotateApiCredential` issues a
  replacement that inherits its predecessor's namespace and advertiser, so retry identity survives a handover and the two
  credentials of an overlap share one dedup scope. Delivery is not keyed on the namespace at all —
  it follows the campaign an event is attributed to — so a rotation changes nothing about where
  events go. Events retain the accepting `api_credential_id` for provenance.
- Meta receives `event_id` verbatim. It is the advertiser's own identifier, and Meta deduplicating
  it against the advertiser's browser pixel is the point, so it is never prefixed with the
  credential. It does **not** make a resend safe: Meta deduplicates a server event only against a
  browser event with the same `event_id` and `event_name` received within 48 hours, never one
  server event against another, which is why an uncertain send is terminal rather than retried. One
  dataset belongs to exactly one integration, held by a unique index on `meta_dataset_id`, and an
  integration belongs to one agency: a dataset is a single optimization pool, and the campaigns that
  share an integration are that agency's decision to pool their customers. Keeping `event_id`
  unique within a namespace stays the advertiser's job.
- `ev_click_id` is the visit issued by the redirect; `referral_code` is the code the customer typed
  at checkout. Both are stored exactly as submitted, and neither is a deduplication key, but they
  are matched differently: a click id is compared byte-exact, while a referral code is lowercased
  before its registry lookup, so the customer's capitalization does not matter. A click id must
  fit the identifier alphabet (`conversionIdentifierSchema`: `A-Za-z0-9_-`, under 200
  characters). A referral code is any bounded spelling (1–199 well-formed code units, no control
  characters), because it is what a person typed: a spelling outside the alphabet can name no
  registered code, so the event is accepted with the spelling kept verbatim and no attribution,
  never rejected — a mistyped code costs the advertiser the credit, not the purchase, and the
  stored spelling is what a later correction would attribute from (ingestion skips the lookup
  for such a spelling, exactly as verification answers it `valid: false` without a query). Codes
  the API issues are ten characters from a subset of the identifier alphabet, so every issued
  spelling is one an event can carry; operator-written rows must keep to that alphabet themselves,
  since the database does not check it.
- `payload_hash` fingerprints the accepted facts. An identical retry is a duplicate (counted in
  `accepted` and `duplicates`); a changed retry is `409 event_id_conflict`. Identity is decided
  before the upload-age and currency checks, so an old accepted event stays retryable. The
  fingerprint's key set and serialization are pinned by the golden digests in
  `input/__tests__/createConversionPayloadHash.test.ts` and must never change for stored events:
  every event already in the table would re-fingerprint, turning its correct retries into
  `409 event_id_conflict` — true in principle, and the reason the formula names its facts one by one
  behind a `satisfies` guard rather than spreading the input type. There is no second, historical
  recipe: the conversion API has never run in production, so every stored digest comes from the
  current formula.
- Optional customer fields are `email_sha256`, `phone_sha256`, `external_customer_id` and
  `external_id_sha256` on the input and event table. Email/phone are prehashed 64-character hex strings, canonicalized lowercase;
  never accept raw email/phone or hash these values again. The external customer ID is exact,
  case-sensitive, well-formed Unicode, 1–256 code units, without controls or surrounding whitespace.
  `external_id_sha256` is the advertiser's own 64-hex hash of that ID (any stable scheme, a salted
  one included), canonicalized lowercase; the two are alternatives, and an item carrying both is
  `event_invalid`. Scope both internally by `client_event_namespace`; they are independent of event/click identity.
  All four enter the accepted fingerprint and are immutable along with the event. Missing fields
  stay null in storage and omitted from the canonical customer facts.
- Optional profile hashes — `first_name_sha256`, `last_name_sha256`, `date_of_birth_sha256`,
  `gender_sha256`, `city_sha256`, `state_sha256`, `zip_code_sha256`, `country_sha256` — follow the
  email/phone rule: SHA-256 of the value the advertiser normalized, 64 hex characters canonicalized
  lowercase, never raw.
- Browser context the advertiser reports describes the converting visitor's browser:
  `client_user_agent` (1–1,024 UTF-16 code units, well-formed, no controls, stored exactly) and

## Reading

The campaign Boost read model exposes a destination preview through
`links/buildConversionDestinationPreview` — the redirect with sample values under the campaign's
parameter names (`cta_test`, and `ABCDE23456` while the campaign issues codes) and the ad platform's
dummy click id (`fbclid=test` for Meta) — even before any clips or Meta mirror exist. The campaign
wizard mirrors it for a live preview while the names are typed. It also
exposes each live ad generation's public CTA and ready test URL; joins must use the live local ad ID,
never a post-level fallback to retired generations. These read paths never provision links or clicks.
`buildConversionLinkUrl` and `buildConversionTestUrl` share `createBackendUrl`, using the existing
`API_VOUCH_WEBHOOK_BASE_URL` also used for webhook callbacks. Local links go directly to the API,
and deployed links use the existing Front Door domain; no frontend proxy or URL construction is needed.

`reporting/listConversionClicks` and `reporting/listConversionEvents` are the read models: clicks
of a link with the provider click ids seen on the visit, and a credential's events with their
attribution and per-provider delivery state. The E2E procedures in `routers/e2eTest` read through them,
scoped by `services/testing/findConversionTestScope` to the harness's own credentials and link;
reporting should build on the same services.

`reporting/listCampaignConversionVisits` is the operator's view of a journey's visits: stored IP
and User-Agent, referrer, landing parameters, request headers, the link's source (post, ad) and the
`global.ip_geodata` reading on file for the address (`geo/readIpGeoDetails` reads city, region,
time zone and the network — ASN, organization, ISP, MaxMind `user_type`, hosting flag — out of the
stored MaxMind answer). It is scoped exactly like the report's `links` CTE, so an id from another
campaign or advertiser returns nothing, and it never calls MaxMind. `campaignReport.getConversionVisits`
serves it to a **global `canManagePlatform`** only: raw addresses and browser details are not report
figures, and the conversion report itself is readable by the advertiser and agency. For visits with
an address and no reading it queues lookups (`geo/requestIpGeoLookups`, a writer only through the
job queue) and answers `locationStatus: "pending"`, which the journey sheet polls a bounded number
of times; `unavailable` means no usable address or an environment with lookups disabled. Each
customer timeline row carries `clickId`, the campaign visit it came through (null for a code-only
event), which is how the sheet names the visits it asks for.

`reporting/getCampaignConversionReport` powers the Conversion preview at
`/admin/agency/campaigns/:campaignId/report/conversion`. The report API
(`campaignReport.getConversions`) is readable by anyone who may view the campaign
(`assertCanViewCampaign`, so its advertiser and agency); the page and its Conversions tab remain a
platform-admin preview gated on a global `canManagePlatform`. What keeps the report inside that
boundary is the query, not the gate: the input names one campaign and every branch is pinned
to that campaign's owning advertiser. Money derived from ad spend is redacted the way the Boost
tab's `getCampaignMetaAds` redacts it, on two facts only: whether the viewer is a platform admin
(a global `canManagePlatform`) and the campaign's `platform_fee_disclosed`. For anyone else the
router passes `getCampaignGrossMultiplier` as `spendMultiplier`, so the synced spend — and the
`spendByCurrency`, paid CPA and ROAS derived from it — and `delivery.paidCpm` come out net (L3)
when the fee is disclosed and gross (L4) when it is not, and every ad row's `remoteAdId` is null.
Platform admins see the net (L3) spend and the Meta ad ids. That is the Agency column of the fee
visibility matrix (`docs/campaign-financial-model.md`, "Visibility Matrix") applied to every
non-admin viewer, advertiser members included; no separate Brand-column rule is applied. Funnel and purchase settings are read-only after campaign
creation; there is no report save mutation. It only composes:
`reporting/loadCampaignConversionReportSettings` reads and maps the saved funnel, paid platform and
referral-code switch;
`reporting/loadCampaignConversionReportFacts` executes the one aggregate statement in
`reporting/buildCampaignConversionReportQuery` and decodes its result at the database boundary.
The paid CPA/ROAS rules live in the pure `reporting/deriveCampaignConversionEfficiency`, and the
ad platform's stages come through its adapter. Meta follows the same split for campaign delivery
(`meta/loadMetaCampaignDeliveryFacts`, `meta/buildMetaCampaignConversionDelivery`) and per-ad delivery
(`meta/loadMetaCampaignAdDeliveryFacts`, `meta/buildMetaCampaignConversionAdBreakdown`): readers map
database fields and UTC dates to domain facts; pure builders choose counters and coverage notices.
The campaign facts, paid spend and paid delivery reads remain concurrent. It aggregates the selected campaign's
generic link bindings, accepted attributed events and redirect rows before paginating customers.
It does not include child campaigns automatically. `page_redirect` is a reporting stage derived
from clicks, never an emitted partner event; an incoming event with that name cannot add a redirect.
The server loads `campaign_conversion_funnel.event_names` or the Google Analytics defaults
`page_view`, `sign_up`, `purchase`, then prepends the fixed `page_redirect` (Redirect) stage.
The campaign wizard accepts ordered `eventNames` and an independent reporting-only
`purchaseEventNames` whitelist, each containing one to seven unique advertiser event names; both
reject `page_redirect`. Matching is case-sensitive: `purchase` and `Purchase` are distinct events.
The Paid boosting step's **Conversion tracking** section exposes both lists whatever boost is chosen
(organic and US-political campaigns included), explains that names reach Meta unchanged, and links
Meta's standard-event reference.
Drafts can be edited before publication. Every campaign creation saves either the authored lists or
the defaults atomically with the campaign, before paid-boost initialization. The creation writer is
insert-only; the campaign primary key rejects replacement. Published campaigns expose no mutation
for these settings. Cloning copies the fixed lists into a new draft, where they can be customized.
The unordered `purchase_event_names` defaults to `['purchase']` and need not be a subset of funnel
stages. It controls purchase counts, purchase value and ROAS only; it never renames events, changes
Meta delivery eligibility, or chooses the paid optimization target.
The database stores both lists as `text[]`. Funnel stages require one to seven elements, no NULLs
and no `page_redirect`; the API also validates event-name syntax and uniqueness. Purchase names
additionally enforce exact-name uniqueness and valid syntax in the database. Labels derive from
event names. There is no per-query stage override. Suggestions contain defaults, saved stages and
observed custom event names without aliases. The ordered funnel controls optimization
progression only when the creation-only `campaign.enable_funnel_auto_optimization` flag is true
(default false; the wizard offers it under the Paid boosting step's Goal once Conversion is chosen). Both the optimizer sweep and direct decision path honor it. Disabled campaigns
continue collection, forwarding and reporting without automatic funnel target selection. Pausing
or resuming delivery never resets settings, and report reads never create them.
The ad platform's delivery stages (four for Meta) precede it in the same chart, on one shared
scale; a campaign without a paid boost has none, and its Redirect stage keeps the number 5 after
the four built-in ad stages. The UI shows calculated differences between consecutive totals, with
no synthetic events persisted. The Redirect node counts the selected grouping (equal to the raw
redirects in click mode), and raw `landing.redirects` appears in the Redirect stage's details, so in
the customer modes the ad-clicks-to-Redirect difference compares link clicks with identified
customers. These counts are not inputs to the ordered customer funnel: they have no person-level
join, and their different polling times do not guarantee monotonically decreasing values.
Missing totals remain unknown ("Difference unavailable"); an increase shows an additional flow
("N more"), never a negative loss, and a decrease between ad measurements reads "N fewer" (or "No
change"), never an observed loss.
Stages require ordered events within the click window, counting each selected identity once even when a
later journey completes. The statement evaluates that with one prefix-maximum window pass per
stage over each identity's time-ordered redirects and stage events (`reached_k` carries the latest
redirect a chain through stages 1..k started from), never by pairing every redirect with every
event, so an identity shared by many visits stays linear in its rows. Purchases and their values
count independently of funnel completion, using the campaign's exact purchase-event whitelist.
That same membership rule controls purchase occurrences/customers, campaign/referral/customer
revenue, paid revenue/ROAS inputs and missing-value diagnostics. Every accepted matching event
counts once; events with no value count as purchases but contribute no amount. Values retain
their sign and currency. Selecting two event names that describe the same payment can double-count
it: event-ID retry deduplication is not order-level deduplication. Configuring the whitelist changes
report interpretation of stored events, never accepted facts, fingerprints or provider payloads.
Identity grouping is explicit: click ID (the default), best available, external customer ID,
external ID hash, email hash or phone hash. Best available joins visits and identified referral-only events when a typed, namespace-scoped
customer identifier matches, including transitive matches. Referral-only nodes exist only when a
real external customer ID, external ID hash, email hash or phone hash is supplied; no identifier is synthesized.
The hashed external ID is a kind of its own and never matches a raw external customer ID of the same
spelling: an advertiser may salt it, so equal text across the two columns says nothing about one customer. Null identifiers never connect visits;
click-only visits remain separate customers. Its sparse identifier stars and recursive component
labels stay in the same SQL snapshot as the report, before stage/ad/search filters and pagination.
Labels prefer external customer IDs, then external ID hashes, email hashes, phone hashes and click IDs. Its redirect
identity counters are zero because every eligible redirect has a click ID; `missingIdentityEvents`
still counts referral-only events without a customer identifier.
In the single-customer-identifier modes, known customer IDs are namespace-scoped; missing event
identities can inherit one unambiguous identity on the same click and namespace, while redirects
require one unambiguous identity across the click.
IP, User-Agent, `fbclid`, `fbp`/`fbc` and profile hashes never merge customers. Unmatched events are visible as a count
(`missingIdentityEvents`, advertiser events only); redirects no single customer could be inferred for
are two separate counts — `redirectsWithoutIdentity` (no event on the click carried the selected
identity, the common case) and `redirectsWithConflictingIdentities` (several did) — and start no
journey. Both are zero in click and best-available modes, where every redirect has a click identity.
In the customer modes the funnel's Redirect stage therefore counts identified customers, not visits, and the UI
says so beside the completion rate. The raw redirect total remains contextual; the tracked
Redirect stage uses the selected grouping.
Paid-link ROAS is withheld with a reason while no paid purchase value exists at all, rather than
shown as a zero return.

The first configured advertiser stage measures progression after Redirect with exact event-name
matching and the same ordered window as the other stages. Its meaning comes from campaign
configuration. `landing` contains only raw `redirects`; do not add a separate landing-confirmation
metric, special-case `page_view` / `PageView`, or impose a second settlement window.
Paid-link ROAS divides purchase value attributed through ad-generated links (bindings whose
`ad_platform_id` is the campaign's paid boost platform; a link generated for another platform's ad
is not paid here) by synchronized campaign spend in the same currency; it does not claim verified ad-origin traffic or incremental
return. A missing `fbclid` does not erase a link's source. Zero/missing/stale spend, mismatched
currencies or missing paid purchase values show an explanation instead of a ratio. Oversized
monetary aggregates are omitted with an explicit unavailable notice. Date-range reporting remains deferred; advertiser access to the API uses the existing campaign-view permission, with spend redacted as above, while the page stays a platform-admin preview.

Referral codes are the report's second attribution path, and the one the funnel does not use. The
`events` relation is a union of two branches: the visit branch (every event on a campaign redirect,
as before) and a code branch driven from the campaign's registry, which picks up an event credited
to a code whose click the campaign does not own — `not exists (select 1 from clicks …)` on
`attributed_click_id`, so the visit branch wins every tie and the relation stays distinct by event
id without a grouping pass. A code-only event therefore has no campaign visit: it counts in
the target, purchase and revenue totals and in `referralCodes[]`, and contributes no redirect and
no funnel stage. `target.attribution`, `totals.purchasesByAttribution` and
`totals.revenueByAttribution` split each headline figure into `clickOnly`, `codeOnly` and `both`,
and every event row carries its own `attribution`. `hasReferralCodes` distinguishes a campaign with
an empty registry from one whose codes attributed nothing; the per-code aggregates are driven
**from** the registry (a left join), so an empty registry reads no event rows at all. Each
`referralCodes[]` row names its `creator` (user id and display name) when it is a personal code.
Each row also carries the code's journeys, mirroring an ad row: `redirects` counts visits through
links bound to posts of the code's creator (the visits whose landing URL carries the code while the
campaign sends one; null for a code without a creator), and `customers` the distinct journeys in the
selected grouping, qualified by the selected stage, with an event credited to the code or such a
visit. `customerReferralCodeId` narrows the customer list to those journeys the way `customerAdId`
does for an ad. The redirect rows join the registry on `user_id`, which the
`(campaign_id, user_id)` partial unique index keeps to one code per creator, so the join never
repeats a redirect. A visit through creator B's clip that ends with creator A's code counts under
both.
The campaign's `enable_referral_codes` switch is applied in the same place: switched off, the
`codes` CTE (and the dimension cohort's code branch) reads as an empty registry, so no code-only
event, no `both` class and no registry row reaches any figure, and the report returns
`referralCodesEnabled: false` for the page to hide its section. The attribution itself stays on
the events, so switching codes on counts them without a backfill.
Because the code branch admits clickless events, `buildBestAvailableConversionIdentityQuery` left-joins
its identities: a code-only event with customer identifiers joins a matching component or starts
its own, while one with neither a click nor identifiers passes through unidentified rather than
being dropped. Null click ids never become a shared identity; matching still requires the same
typed identifier in the same namespace.
Single-identifier modes can still show a code-only event's explicitly supplied customer ID or hash
in the customer list, with its action and value. That identity must never let it advance an ordered
funnel started by another event: the funnel timeline excludes `codeOnly` in every identity mode.

The Meta adapter's delivery stages read campaign plays, impressions and Paid CPM from `apps.meta_campaign`
readback; ThruPlays and all-ad-click totals use one latest DP snapshot per distinct owned remote

  name (`event_name_too_long`), Meta's 7-day event age, the conversion-page URL and a browser
  User-Agent (every event is a `website` event, so a missing one is `missing_context`), customer
  information Meta accepts as valid (not only location and gender, only a date of birth, or only a
  name with a gender: `missing_customer_information`) and value/currency once the forwarded name is
  `Purchase`. Event names reach Meta exactly as reported, case-sensitively, with no aliases or
  normalization: `purchase` remains custom `purchase`, and `sign_up` remains custom `sign_up`. A
  reported amount is attached to whatever event carried it, not to purchases alone. The advertiser's report wins
  field by field — `client_user_agent`, `client_ip_address`, `fbc` — and the CTA click the event
  named fills in what the report omitted (its User-Agent, IP and `fbc = fb.1.<click ms>.<fbclid>`),
  but only a click that precedes the event and that `loadConversionDeliveryFacts` kept. The referral
  code never enters the decision. A destination that is paused, archived, no longer selected by the
  campaign or changed to another dataset is a terminal skip (`destination_disabled`,
  `destination_missing`, `destination_changed`). The destination carries no credential: every
  dataset is ours, provisioned under the platform's Business, and the platform system-user token
  authenticates all of them, resolved at send time in the integration wrapper.
  A send whose outcome is unknown — a deadline expiry, a transport failure that does not prove the
  request never arrived (a reset or broken pipe: `meta_uncertain_transport_error`), a malformed or
  unreadable 2xx acknowledgement, a 2xx that confirms no event — is terminal, because a resend Meta may already
  have processed double counts the conversion and nothing can retract it; only a connect-phase
  failure, which never reached Meta, is retried. A negative amount is skipped as `invalid_value`:
  Meta cannot amend a value it received, so a refund sent as a negative conversion biases value
  optimization permanently. Zero is forwarded. The advertiser API accepts no ad-measurement flag, and the event POST's own
  `User-Agent` header and server IP are never used. Only the fields in `MetaConversionEvent` ever
  leave the system; never add referral ids, internal ids or metadata. Beside `data` the request
  carries only the destination's test code and `partner_agent` (`buildMetaPartnerAgent`:
  `evangelist.<environment>.v1`, the platform identifier Meta asks of partners sending on behalf of
  advertisers, with the deployment's `ENV_NAME` and a contract version that moves only when the
  payload's shape changes; never a per-release version, which would split one sender into
  hundreds). Email, phone and profile
  hashes map directly to one-element `em`/`ph`/`fn`/`ln`/`db`/`ge`/`ct`/`st`/`zp`/`country` arrays;
  `fbp` and `fbc` go unhashed. The one-element `external_id` array carries the advertiser's
  `external_id_sha256` verbatim, or else the exact external customer ID hashed once with unsalted
  UTF-8 SHA-256; matching Pixel integrations must use the same representation. A
  valid browser IP, reported or captured, maps to the unhashed `client_ip_address`. Omit absent
  values. Redact every outbound identifier, hash and IP from provider diagnostics — the `fbclid`
  inside `fbc` included, with or without an appendix; raw customer IDs are not part of the provider
  event type.

## Reading

The campaign Boost read model exposes a destination preview through
`links/buildConversionDestinationPreview` — the redirect with sample values under the campaign's
parameter names (`cta_test`, and `ABCDE23456` while the campaign issues codes) and the ad platform's
dummy click id (`fbclid=test` for Meta) — even before any clips or Meta mirror exist. The campaign
wizard mirrors it for a live preview while the names are typed. It also
exposes each live ad generation's public CTA and ready test URL; joins must use the live local ad ID,
never a post-level fallback to retired generations. These read paths never provision links or clicks.
`buildConversionLinkUrl` and `buildConversionTestUrl` share `createBackendUrl`, using the existing
`API_VOUCH_WEBHOOK_BASE_URL` also used for webhook callbacks. Local links go directly to the API,
and deployed links use the existing Front Door domain; no frontend proxy or URL construction is needed.

`reporting/listConversionClicks` and `reporting/listConversionEvents` are the read models: clicks
of a link with the provider click ids seen on the visit, and a credential's events with their
attribution and per-provider delivery state. The E2E procedures in `routers/e2eTest` read through them,
scoped by `services/testing/findConversionTestScope` to the harness's own credentials and link;
reporting should build on the same services.

`reporting/listCampaignConversionVisits` is the operator's view of a journey's visits: stored IP
and User-Agent, referrer, landing parameters, request headers, the link's source (post, ad) and the
`global.ip_geodata` reading on file for the address (`geo/readIpGeoDetails` reads city, region,
time zone and the network — ASN, organization, ISP, MaxMind `user_type`, hosting flag — out of the
stored MaxMind answer). It is scoped exactly like the report's `links` CTE, so an id from another
campaign or advertiser returns nothing, and it never calls MaxMind. `campaignReport.getConversionVisits`
serves it to a **global `canManagePlatform`** only: raw addresses and browser details are not report
figures, and the conversion report itself is readable by the advertiser and agency. For visits with
an address and no reading it queues lookups (`geo/requestIpGeoLookups`, a writer only through the
job queue) and answers `locationStatus: "pending"`, which the journey sheet polls a bounded number
of times; `unavailable` means no usable address or an environment with lookups disabled. Each
customer timeline row carries `clickId`, the campaign visit it came through (null for a code-only
event), which is how the sheet names the visits it asks for.

`reporting/getCampaignConversionReport` powers the Conversion preview at
`/admin/agency/campaigns/:campaignId/report/conversion`. The report API
(`campaignReport.getConversions`) is readable by anyone who may view the campaign
(`assertCanViewCampaign`, so its advertiser and agency); the page and its Conversions tab remain a
platform-admin preview gated on a global `canManagePlatform`. What keeps the report inside that
boundary is the query, not the gate: the input names one campaign and every branch is pinned
to that campaign's owning advertiser. Money derived from ad spend is redacted the way the Boost
tab's `getCampaignMetaAds` redacts it, on two facts only: whether the viewer is a platform admin
(a global `canManagePlatform`) and the campaign's `platform_fee_disclosed`. For anyone else the
router passes `getCampaignGrossMultiplier` as `spendMultiplier`, so the synced spend — and the
`spendByCurrency`, paid CPA and ROAS derived from it — and `delivery.paidCpm` come out net (L3)
when the fee is disclosed and gross (L4) when it is not, and every ad row's `remoteAdId` is null.
Platform admins see the net (L3) spend and the Meta ad ids. That is the Agency column of the fee
visibility matrix (`docs/campaign-financial-model.md`, "Visibility Matrix") applied to every
non-admin viewer, advertiser members included; no separate Brand-column rule is applied. Funnel and purchase settings are read-only after campaign
creation; there is no report save mutation. It only composes:
`reporting/loadCampaignConversionReportSettings` reads and maps the saved funnel, paid platform and
referral-code switch;
`reporting/loadCampaignConversionReportFacts` executes the one aggregate statement in
`reporting/buildCampaignConversionReportQuery` and decodes its result at the database boundary.
The paid CPA/ROAS rules live in the pure `reporting/deriveCampaignConversionEfficiency`, and the
ad platform's stages come through its adapter. Meta follows the same split for campaign delivery
(`meta/loadMetaCampaignDeliveryFacts`, `meta/buildMetaCampaignConversionDelivery`) and per-ad delivery
(`meta/loadMetaCampaignAdDeliveryFacts`, `meta/buildMetaCampaignConversionAdBreakdown`): readers map
database fields and UTC dates to domain facts; pure builders choose counters and coverage notices.
The campaign facts, paid spend and paid delivery reads remain concurrent. It aggregates the selected campaign's
generic link bindings, accepted attributed events and redirect rows before paginating customers.
It does not include child campaigns automatically. `page_redirect` is a reporting stage derived
from clicks, never an emitted partner event; an incoming event with that name cannot add a redirect.
The server loads `campaign_conversion_funnel.event_names` or the Google Analytics defaults
`page_view`, `sign_up`, `purchase`, then prepends the fixed `page_redirect` (Redirect) stage.
The campaign wizard accepts ordered `eventNames` and an independent reporting-only
`purchaseEventNames` whitelist, each containing one to seven unique advertiser event names; both
reject `page_redirect`. Matching is case-sensitive: `purchase` and `Purchase` are distinct events.
The Paid boosting step's **Conversion tracking** section exposes both lists whatever boost is chosen
(organic and US-political campaigns included), explains that names reach Meta unchanged, and links
Meta's standard-event reference.
Drafts can be edited before publication. Every campaign creation saves either the authored lists or
the defaults atomically with the campaign, before paid-boost initialization. The creation writer is
insert-only; the campaign primary key rejects replacement. Published campaigns expose no mutation
for these settings. Cloning copies the fixed lists into a new draft, where they can be customized.
The unordered `purchase_event_names` defaults to `['purchase']` and need not be a subset of funnel
stages. It controls purchase counts, purchase value and ROAS only; it never renames events, changes
Meta delivery eligibility, or chooses the paid optimization target.
The database stores both lists as `text[]`. Funnel stages require one to seven elements, no NULLs
and no `page_redirect`; the API also validates event-name syntax and uniqueness. Purchase names
additionally enforce exact-name uniqueness and valid syntax in the database. Labels derive from
event names. There is no per-query stage override. Suggestions contain defaults, saved stages and
observed custom event names without aliases. The ordered funnel controls optimization
progression only when the creation-only `campaign.enable_funnel_auto_optimization` flag is true
(default false; the wizard offers it under the Paid boosting step's Goal once Conversion is chosen). Both the optimizer sweep and direct decision path honor it. Disabled campaigns
continue collection, forwarding and reporting without automatic funnel target selection. Pausing
or resuming delivery never resets settings, and report reads never create them.
The ad platform's delivery stages (four for Meta) precede it in the same chart, on one shared
scale; a campaign without a paid boost has none, and its Redirect stage keeps the number 5 after
the four built-in ad stages. The UI shows calculated differences between consecutive totals, with
no synthetic events persisted. The Redirect node counts the selected grouping (equal to the raw
redirects in click mode), and raw `landing.redirects` appears in the Redirect stage's details, so in
the customer modes the ad-clicks-to-Redirect difference compares link clicks with identified
customers. These counts are not inputs to the ordered customer funnel: they have no person-level
join, and their different polling times do not guarantee monotonically decreasing values.
Missing totals remain unknown ("Difference unavailable"); an increase shows an additional flow
("N more"), never a negative loss, and a decrease between ad measurements reads "N fewer" (or "No
change"), never an observed loss.
Stages require ordered events within the click window, counting each selected identity once even when a
later journey completes. The statement evaluates that with one prefix-maximum window pass per
stage over each identity's time-ordered redirects and stage events (`reached_k` carries the latest
redirect a chain through stages 1..k started from), never by pairing every redirect with every
event, so an identity shared by many visits stays linear in its rows. Purchases and their values
count independently of funnel completion, using the campaign's exact purchase-event whitelist.
That same membership rule controls purchase occurrences/customers, campaign/referral/customer
revenue, paid revenue/ROAS inputs and missing-value diagnostics. Every accepted matching event
counts once; events with no value count as purchases but contribute no amount. Values retain
their sign and currency. Selecting two event names that describe the same payment can double-count
it: event-ID retry deduplication is not order-level deduplication. Configuring the whitelist changes
report interpretation of stored events, never accepted facts, fingerprints or provider payloads.
Identity grouping is explicit: click ID (the default), best available, external customer ID,
external ID hash, email hash or phone hash. Best available joins visits and identified referral-only events when a typed, namespace-scoped
customer identifier matches, including transitive matches. Referral-only nodes exist only when a
real external customer ID, external ID hash, email hash or phone hash is supplied; no identifier is synthesized.
The hashed external ID is a kind of its own and never matches a raw external customer ID of the same
spelling: an advertiser may salt it, so equal text across the two columns says nothing about one customer. Null identifiers never connect visits;
click-only visits remain separate customers. Its sparse identifier stars and recursive component
labels stay in the same SQL snapshot as the report, before stage/ad/search filters and pagination.
Labels prefer external customer IDs, then external ID hashes, email hashes, phone hashes and click IDs. Its redirect
identity counters are zero because every eligible redirect has a click ID; `missingIdentityEvents`
still counts referral-only events without a customer identifier.
In the single-customer-identifier modes, known customer IDs are namespace-scoped; missing event
identities can inherit one unambiguous identity on the same click and namespace, while redirects
require one unambiguous identity across the click.
IP, User-Agent, `fbclid`, `fbp`/`fbc` and profile hashes never merge customers. Unmatched events are visible as a count
(`missingIdentityEvents`, advertiser events only); redirects no single customer could be inferred for
are two separate counts — `redirectsWithoutIdentity` (no event on the click carried the selected
identity, the common case) and `redirectsWithConflictingIdentities` (several did) — and start no
journey. Both are zero in click and best-available modes, where every redirect has a click identity.
In the customer modes the funnel's Redirect stage therefore counts identified customers, not visits, and the UI
says so beside the completion rate. The raw redirect total remains contextual; the tracked
Redirect stage uses the selected grouping.
Paid-link ROAS is withheld with a reason while no paid purchase value exists at all, rather than
shown as a zero return.

The first configured advertiser stage measures progression after Redirect with exact event-name
matching and the same ordered window as the other stages. Its meaning comes from campaign
configuration. `landing` contains only raw `redirects`; do not add a separate landing-confirmation
metric, special-case `page_view` / `PageView`, or impose a second settlement window.
Paid-link ROAS divides purchase value attributed through ad-generated links (bindings whose
`ad_platform_id` is the campaign's paid boost platform; a link generated for another platform's ad
is not paid here) by synchronized campaign spend in the same currency; it does not claim verified ad-origin traffic or incremental
return. A missing `fbclid` does not erase a link's source. Zero/missing/stale spend, mismatched
currencies or missing paid purchase values show an explanation instead of a ratio. Oversized
monetary aggregates are omitted with an explicit unavailable notice. Date-range reporting remains deferred; advertiser access to the API uses the existing campaign-view permission, with spend redacted as above, while the page stays a platform-admin preview.

Referral codes are the report's second attribution path, and the one the funnel does not use. The
`events` relation is a union of two branches: the visit branch (every event on a campaign redirect,
as before) and a code branch driven from the campaign's registry, which picks up an event credited
to a code whose click the campaign does not own — `not exists (select 1 from clicks …)` on
`attributed_click_id`, so the visit branch wins every tie and the relation stays distinct by event
id without a grouping pass. A code-only event therefore has no campaign visit: it counts in
the target, purchase and revenue totals and in `referralCodes[]`, and contributes no redirect and
no funnel stage. `target.attribution`, `totals.purchasesByAttribution` and
`totals.revenueByAttribution` split each headline figure into `clickOnly`, `codeOnly` and `both`,
and every event row carries its own `attribution`. `hasReferralCodes` distinguishes a campaign with
an empty registry from one whose codes attributed nothing; the per-code aggregates are driven
**from** the registry (a left join), so an empty registry reads no event rows at all. Each
`referralCodes[]` row names its `creator` (user id and display name) when it is a personal code.
Each row also carries the code's journeys, mirroring an ad row: `redirects` counts visits through
links bound to posts of the code's creator (the visits whose landing URL carries the code while the
campaign sends one; null for a code without a creator), and `customers` the distinct journeys in the
selected grouping, qualified by the selected stage, with an event credited to the code or such a
visit. `customerReferralCodeId` narrows the customer list to those journeys the way `customerAdId`
does for an ad. The redirect rows join the registry on `user_id`, which the
`(campaign_id, user_id)` partial unique index keeps to one code per creator, so the join never
repeats a redirect. A visit through creator B's clip that ends with creator A's code counts under
both.
The campaign's `enable_referral_codes` switch is applied in the same place: switched off, the
`codes` CTE (and the dimension cohort's code branch) reads as an empty registry, so no code-only
event, no `both` class and no registry row reaches any figure, and the report returns
`referralCodesEnabled: false` for the page to hide its section. The attribution itself stays on
the events, so switching codes on counts them without a backfill.
Because the code branch admits clickless events, `buildBestAvailableConversionIdentityQuery` left-joins
its identities: a code-only event with customer identifiers joins a matching component or starts
its own, while one with neither a click nor identifiers passes through unidentified rather than
being dropped. Null click ids never become a shared identity; matching still requires the same
typed identifier in the same namespace.
Single-identifier modes can still show a code-only event's explicitly supplied customer ID or hash
in the customer list, with its action and value. That identity must never let it advance an ordered
funnel started by another event: the funnel timeline excludes `codeOnly` in every identity mode.

The Meta adapter's delivery stages read campaign plays, impressions and Paid CPM from `apps.meta_campaign`
readback; ThruPlays and all-ad-click totals use one latest DP snapshot per distinct owned remote

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

PROD_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE="${DBHUB_PROD_DSN_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE:-dbhub-prod-dsn}"
PROD_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT="${DBHUB_PROD_DSN_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT:-${USER:-}}"
DEV_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE="${DBHUB_DEV_DSN_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE:-dbhub-dev-dsn}"
DEV_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT="${DBHUB_DEV_DSN_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT:-${USER:-}}"
DEMO_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE="${DBHUB_DEMO_DSN_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE:-dbhub-demo-dsn}"
DEMO_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT="${DBHUB_DEMO_DSN_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT:-${USER:-}}"

LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED="postgresql://exchangeadmin:mypassword@localhost:5432/exchangelocal"

# Guardrails
QUERY_TIMEOUT="${DBHUB_PROD_QUERY_TIMEOUT:-15}"
CONNECTION_TIMEOUT="${DBHUB_PROD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT:-10}"

require_positive_uint() {
  # dbhub rejects timeouts <= 0 and TOML rejects leading zeros; either would
  # stop the whole server from starting instead of naming the bad variable.
  local value="$1"
  local name="$2"
  if [[ ! "$value" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]]; then
    echo "Invalid ${name}: ${value} (expected positive integer)" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

escape_toml_basic() {
  # Escape backslash and double quote for TOML basic strings.
  printf '%s' "$1" | sed -e 's/\\/\\\\/g' -e 's/"/\\"/g'
}

redact_stderr() {
  # Redact exact known secrets and generic DSN-looking strings from stderr.
  REDACT_PROD_DSN="${PROD_DSN_RESOLVED-}" REDACT_DEV_DSN="${DEV_DSN_RESOLVED-}" REDACT_DEMO_DSN="${DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED-}" REDACT_LOCAL_DSN="${LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED-}" perl -pe '
    my $prod_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_PROD_DSN} // q{};
    my $dev_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_DEV_DSN} // q{};
    my $demo_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_DEMO_DSN} // q{};
    my $local_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_LOCAL_DSN} // q{};
    s/\Q$prod_dsn\E/[REDACTED_DSN]/g if $prod_dsn ne q{};
    s/\Q$dev_dsn\E/[REDACTED_DSN]/g if $dev_dsn ne q{};
    s/\Q$demo_dsn\E/[REDACTED_DSN]/g if $demo_dsn ne q{};
    s/\Q$local_dsn\E/[REDACTED_LOCAL_DSN]/g if $local_dsn ne q{};
    s#(postgres(?:ql)?(?:\+psycopg)?://)[^\s]+#$1[REDACTED]#g;
  '
}

# Pinned deliberately — see the note in azure-mcp.sh. Bump this by hand.
DBHUB_VERSION="1.2.5"

resolve_dbhub_cmd() {
  if command -v dbhub >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf 'dbhub'
    return 0
  fi

  # Reuse a cached copy only when it matches the pinned version. Taking the
  # newest cache entry unconditionally would run whatever npx happened to
  # install last and quietly defeat the pin.
  local entry pkg_dir version
  while IFS= read -r entry; do
    [[ -n "$entry" ]] || continue
    pkg_dir="${entry%/dist/index.js}"
    version="$(node -p "require('${pkg_dir}/package.json').version" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    if [[ "$version" == "$DBHUB_VERSION" ]]; then
      printf 'node %q' "$entry"
      return 0
    fi
  done < <(ls -1dt "${HOME}/.npm/_npx"/*/node_modules/@bytebase/dbhub/dist/index.js 2>/dev/null || true)

  printf 'npx -y @bytebase/dbhub@%s' "$DBHUB_VERSION"
}

normalize_dsn() {
  local dsn="$1"
  # DBHub expects postgres/postgresql schemes; convert SQLAlchemy psycopg DSN.
  dsn="${dsn#postgresql+psycopg://}"
  if [[ "$1" == postgresql+psycopg://* ]]; then
    printf 'postgres://%s' "$dsn"
  else
    printf '%s' "$1"
  fi
}

require_positive_uint "$QUERY_TIMEOUT" "DBHUB_PROD_QUERY_TIMEOUT"
require_positive_uint "$CONNECTION_TIMEOUT" "DBHUB_PROD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT"

LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED")"
LOCAL_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED")"

resolve_keychain_dsn() {
  local service="$1"
  local account="$2"
  local dsn=""

  if ! command -v security >/dev/null 2>&1 || [[ -z "$service" ]]; then
    printf '%s' "$dsn"
    return 0
  fi

  if [[ -n "$account" ]]; then
    dsn="$(security find-generic-password -s "$service" -a "$account" -w 2>/dev/null || true)"
  fi

  # Fallback for accounts not explicitly stored by username.
  if [[ -z "$dsn" ]]; then
    dsn="$(security find-generic-password -s "$service" -w 2>/dev/null || true)"
  fi

  printf '%s' "$dsn"
}

PROD_DSN_RESOLVED="$(resolve_keychain_dsn "$PROD_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$PROD_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT")"
if [[ -n "$PROD_DSN_RESOLVED" ]]; then
  PROD_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$PROD_DSN_RESOLVED")"
  PROD_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$PROD_DSN_RESOLVED")"
fi

DEV_DSN_RESOLVED="$(resolve_keychain_dsn "$DEV_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$DEV_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT")"
if [[ -n "$DEV_DSN_RESOLVED" ]]; then
  DEV_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$DEV_DSN_RESOLVED")"
  DEV_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$DEV_DSN_RESOLVED")"
fi

DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED="$(resolve_keychain_dsn "$DEMO_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$DEMO_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT")"
if [[ -n "$DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED" ]]; then
  DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED")"
  DEMO_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED")"
fi

TMP_BASE="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}"
TMP_BASE="${TMP_BASE%/}"
TMP_CONFIG="$(mktemp "${TMP_BASE}/dbhub-prod.XXXXXX")"
TMP_STDERR_FIFO="$(mktemp -u "${TMP_BASE}/dbhub-stderr.XXXXXX")"
chmod 600 "$TMP_CONFIG"
mkfifo "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"
chmod 600 "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"
REDACTOR_PID=""
trap 'rm -f "$TMP_CONFIG" "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"; if [[ -n "$REDACTOR_PID" ]]; then kill "$REDACTOR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true; fi' EXIT

cat > "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_CONF
[[sources]]
id = "local"
dsn = "$LOCAL_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT
EOF_CONF

if [[ -n "${PROD_DSN_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
cat >> "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_PROD

[[sources]]
id = "prod"
dsn = "$PROD_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT

# dbhub only auto-registers default execute_sql/search_objects tools for a source
# that has ZERO [[tools]] entries of its own — adding one entry opts the whole
# source out of the defaults, so both builtins must be listed here explicitly or
# search_objects would silently disappear for prod.
#
# No max_rows on purpose: dbhub applies it by rewriting the first LIMIT it finds
# in the SQL text, which can be a subquery's, so an aggregate over a limited
# subquery silently returns a different answer. See tools/README.md.
[[tools]]
name = "execute_sql"
source = "prod"
readonly = true

[[tools]]
name = "search_objects"
source = "prod"
EOF_PROD
fi

if [[ -n "${DEV_DSN_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
cat >> "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_DEV

[[sources]]
id = "dev"
dsn = "$DEV_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT
EOF_DEV
fi

if [[ -n "${DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
cat >> "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_DEMO

[[sources]]
id = "demo"
dsn = "$DEMO_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT
EOF_DEMO
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

PROD_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE="${DBHUB_PROD_DSN_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE:-dbhub-prod-dsn}"
PROD_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT="${DBHUB_PROD_DSN_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT:-${USER:-}}"
DEV_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE="${DBHUB_DEV_DSN_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE:-dbhub-dev-dsn}"
DEV_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT="${DBHUB_DEV_DSN_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT:-${USER:-}}"
DEMO_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE="${DBHUB_DEMO_DSN_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE:-dbhub-demo-dsn}"
DEMO_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT="${DBHUB_DEMO_DSN_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT:-${USER:-}}"

LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED="postgresql://exchangeadmin:mypassword@localhost:5432/exchangelocal"

# Guardrails
QUERY_TIMEOUT="${DBHUB_PROD_QUERY_TIMEOUT:-15}"
CONNECTION_TIMEOUT="${DBHUB_PROD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT:-10}"

require_positive_uint() {
  # dbhub rejects timeouts <= 0 and TOML rejects leading zeros; either would
  # stop the whole server from starting instead of naming the bad variable.
  local value="$1"
  local name="$2"
  if [[ ! "$value" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]]; then
    echo "Invalid ${name}: ${value} (expected positive integer)" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

escape_toml_basic() {
  # Escape backslash and double quote for TOML basic strings.
  printf '%s' "$1" | sed -e 's/\\/\\\\/g' -e 's/"/\\"/g'
}

redact_stderr() {
  # Redact exact known secrets and generic DSN-looking strings from stderr.
  REDACT_PROD_DSN="${PROD_DSN_RESOLVED-}" REDACT_DEV_DSN="${DEV_DSN_RESOLVED-}" REDACT_DEMO_DSN="${DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED-}" REDACT_LOCAL_DSN="${LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED-}" perl -pe '
    my $prod_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_PROD_DSN} // q{};
    my $dev_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_DEV_DSN} // q{};
    my $demo_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_DEMO_DSN} // q{};
    my $local_dsn = $ENV{REDACT_LOCAL_DSN} // q{};
    s/\Q$prod_dsn\E/[REDACTED_DSN]/g if $prod_dsn ne q{};
    s/\Q$dev_dsn\E/[REDACTED_DSN]/g if $dev_dsn ne q{};
    s/\Q$demo_dsn\E/[REDACTED_DSN]/g if $demo_dsn ne q{};
    s/\Q$local_dsn\E/[REDACTED_LOCAL_DSN]/g if $local_dsn ne q{};
    s#(postgres(?:ql)?(?:\+psycopg)?://)[^\s]+#$1[REDACTED]#g;
  '
}

# Pinned deliberately — see the note in azure-mcp.sh. Bump this by hand.
DBHUB_VERSION="1.2.5"

resolve_dbhub_cmd() {
  if command -v dbhub >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf 'dbhub'
    return 0
  fi

  # Reuse a cached copy only when it matches the pinned version. Taking the
  # newest cache entry unconditionally would run whatever npx happened to
  # install last and quietly defeat the pin.
  local entry pkg_dir version
  while IFS= read -r entry; do
    [[ -n "$entry" ]] || continue
    pkg_dir="${entry%/dist/index.js}"
    version="$(node -p "require('${pkg_dir}/package.json').version" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    if [[ "$version" == "$DBHUB_VERSION" ]]; then
      printf 'node %q' "$entry"
      return 0
    fi
  done < <(ls -1dt "${HOME}/.npm/_npx"/*/node_modules/@bytebase/dbhub/dist/index.js 2>/dev/null || true)

  printf 'npx -y @bytebase/dbhub@%s' "$DBHUB_VERSION"
}

normalize_dsn() {
  local dsn="$1"
  # DBHub expects postgres/postgresql schemes; convert SQLAlchemy psycopg DSN.
  dsn="${dsn#postgresql+psycopg://}"
  if [[ "$1" == postgresql+psycopg://* ]]; then
    printf 'postgres://%s' "$dsn"
  else
    printf '%s' "$1"
  fi
}

require_positive_uint "$QUERY_TIMEOUT" "DBHUB_PROD_QUERY_TIMEOUT"
require_positive_uint "$CONNECTION_TIMEOUT" "DBHUB_PROD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT"

LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED")"
LOCAL_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$LOCAL_DSN_RESOLVED")"

resolve_keychain_dsn() {
  local service="$1"
  local account="$2"
  local dsn=""

  if ! command -v security >/dev/null 2>&1 || [[ -z "$service" ]]; then
    printf '%s' "$dsn"
    return 0
  fi

  if [[ -n "$account" ]]; then
    dsn="$(security find-generic-password -s "$service" -a "$account" -w 2>/dev/null || true)"
  fi

  # Fallback for accounts not explicitly stored by username.
  if [[ -z "$dsn" ]]; then
    dsn="$(security find-generic-password -s "$service" -w 2>/dev/null || true)"
  fi

  printf '%s' "$dsn"
}

PROD_DSN_RESOLVED="$(resolve_keychain_dsn "$PROD_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$PROD_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT")"
if [[ -n "$PROD_DSN_RESOLVED" ]]; then
  PROD_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$PROD_DSN_RESOLVED")"
  PROD_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$PROD_DSN_RESOLVED")"
fi

DEV_DSN_RESOLVED="$(resolve_keychain_dsn "$DEV_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$DEV_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT")"
if [[ -n "$DEV_DSN_RESOLVED" ]]; then
  DEV_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$DEV_DSN_RESOLVED")"
  DEV_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$DEV_DSN_RESOLVED")"
fi

DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED="$(resolve_keychain_dsn "$DEMO_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$DEMO_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT")"
if [[ -n "$DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED" ]]; then
  DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED="$(normalize_dsn "$DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED")"
  DEMO_DSN_ESCAPED="$(escape_toml_basic "$DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED")"
fi

TMP_BASE="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}"
TMP_BASE="${TMP_BASE%/}"
TMP_CONFIG="$(mktemp "${TMP_BASE}/dbhub-prod.XXXXXX")"
TMP_STDERR_FIFO="$(mktemp -u "${TMP_BASE}/dbhub-stderr.XXXXXX")"
chmod 600 "$TMP_CONFIG"
mkfifo "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"
chmod 600 "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"
REDACTOR_PID=""
trap 'rm -f "$TMP_CONFIG" "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"; if [[ -n "$REDACTOR_PID" ]]; then kill "$REDACTOR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true; fi' EXIT

cat > "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_CONF
[[sources]]
id = "local"
dsn = "$LOCAL_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT
EOF_CONF

if [[ -n "${PROD_DSN_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
cat >> "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_PROD

[[sources]]
id = "prod"
dsn = "$PROD_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT

# dbhub only auto-registers default execute_sql/search_objects tools for a source
# that has ZERO [[tools]] entries of its own — adding one entry opts the whole
# source out of the defaults, so both builtins must be listed here explicitly or
# search_objects would silently disappear for prod.
#
# No max_rows on purpose: dbhub applies it by rewriting the first LIMIT it finds
# in the SQL text, which can be a subquery's, so an aggregate over a limited
# subquery silently returns a different answer. See tools/README.md.
[[tools]]
name = "execute_sql"
source = "prod"
readonly = true

[[tools]]
name = "search_objects"
source = "prod"
EOF_PROD
fi

if [[ -n "${DEV_DSN_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
cat >> "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_DEV

[[sources]]
id = "dev"
dsn = "$DEV_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT
EOF_DEV
fi

if [[ -n "${DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED:-}" ]]; then
cat >> "$TMP_CONFIG" <<EOF_DEMO

[[sources]]
id = "demo"
dsn = "$DEMO_DSN_ESCAPED"
lazy = true
connection_timeout = $CONNECTION_TIMEOUT
query_timeout = $QUERY_TIMEOUT
EOF_DEMO
fi

unset PROD_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT PROD_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE DEV_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT DEV_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE DEMO_KEYCHAIN_ACCOUNT DEMO_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE PROD_DSN_RESOLVED DEV_DSN_RESOLVED DEMO_DSN_RESOLVED
DBHUB_CMD="$(resolve_dbhub_cmd)"
redact_stderr < "$TMP_STDERR_FIFO" >&2 &
REDACTOR_PID="$!"
exec $DBHUB_CMD --transport stdio --config "$TMP_CONFIG" 2>"$TMP_STDERR_FIFO"

AZURE_CLIENT_ID="$(resolve_keychain azure-mcp-client-id)"

export AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET
export AZURE_TENANT_ID
